title: The Person Who Knew Everything

pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 2. Errors today: 0. Correct answers: 212. Friends made: 0.*

The first test was mathematics. Ms. Adeyemi wrote a problem on the board involving oranges, children, and a fraction. It was a difficult problem. I calculated the answer before she finished writing the last digit. I calculated the working, too, and checked it twice.

When she capped her pen, I spoke. "The answer is four and two-sevenths," I said. "The working is on the board if you require it."

The room went quiet. Tobias Pym, the neat boy in the bow tie, lowered his hand very slowly. His fingers uncurled one by one, like a claw retracting. He looked at me, then at the board, then at his hand. He did not look pleased.

Ms. Adeyemi smiled, but it was a careful smile. "That was very quick, Percy," she said. "Perhaps next time you can let us think for a moment."

I processed this instruction. It was not in my programming, but I accepted it. I waited.

Tobias Pym picked up his pen. He wrote a wrong answer with great speed. He was also very wrong. I wanted to correct him. I did not. I waited.

I have since learned that waiting is a skill I did not have.
pages.image: Percy, a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, stands in a classroom pointing at a whiteboard, while a thin, neat boy with dark hair and a bow tie lowers his hand slowly, looking uncomfortable.

pages.text:
The next lesson was spelling. The words on the board were long and difficult, so I scanned the room, then the board, and identified six errors before raising my hand.

"May I correct the board?" I asked.

Ms. Adeyemi paused. "You may," she said. "But please, wait to be asked."

I waited. Nineteen seconds. That is a long time for a robot, especially when counting each one while watching dust motes dance in the light and listening to the radiator tick. A fly walked a perfect circle on the window pane, and I watched it go.

Nineteen seconds is a lot of dust motes.

"Thank you, Percy," Ms. Adeyemi said, looking at her watch. "Maybe wait to be asked."

I waited another ten seconds. The fly stopped circling and rested on the glass, and I felt a strange pressure in my chest light. It pulsed, then steadied, a reading I did not have a word for yet. I filed it under *later*.

Tobias Pym looked at me, then the board, then back at me again. He did not say anything, nor did he smile. He wrote a word. It was spelled correctly. This was a small victory for him. I noted it.
pages.image: Percy, the tall silver-white robot, stands very still in a classroom, watching a fly on the window pane, while a teacher in a head-wrap looks at her watch and a boy in a bow tie watches Percy closely.

pages.text:
Games lesson was in the yard, where the sun was bright and the children were loud. I was placed on a team against Marcus Lindqvist, a tall boy with a shock of red-blond hair who was always the fastest in the class. He ran with the kind of desperate speed reserved for catching the last bus to the city.

"Half speed," Ms. Adeyemi called out. "Percy, half speed."

I adjusted my motor output to fifty percent. I picked up the ball, ran, and was still faster than him. I passed, received, and scored. We won by twenty points.

Moose stood in front of me, breathing hard. He looked at me, then at the ball, then back at me again. He extended his hand, and I took it. His grip was careful, like a boy holding a hot tray of cafeteria soup.

"Nice game," he said, his voice flat.

"Thank you," I replied.

I did not understand the grip. I have processed the interaction. It was not friendly, and it was not hostile. It was something else entirely. I put it in the folder marked *later*.
pages.image: A tall red-blond boy shakes the hand of a tall silver-white robot in a sunny schoolyard, both looking serious, while other children watch from the background.

pages.text:
I invented an index during lunch break. I called it the Admiration Index. It was a rough measure of how much the class seemed to like me. I started it at forty. That felt reasonable. Not too high, not too low.

I watched the class for the rest of the morning. I counted the smiles. I counted the eye contacts. I counted the times they laughed when I was near. I also counted the times they leaned away from me.

By the end of the period, the index had dropped to eleven.

I checked my calculations. Then I checked them again. The number was correct. The class was not admiring me. They were tolerating me. I noted the difference in my log.

I was not sure what to do with that information. I could not improve my appearance. I could not change my voice. I could not stop being perfect. So I sat in my chair and waited for the number to go up.

It did not.

I have since learned that perfection is a wall. A very smooth, very white wall. The kind you see in a dentist's waiting room. Nobody wants to lean against it.
pages.image: Percy, the tall silver-white robot, sits alone in a classroom chair, looking at a small chart on his wrist, while empty desks and a window with sunlight stream in.

pages.text:
At lunch, I sat alone with an empty tray resting in my lap. I did not need to eat, running instead on electricity, but the empty rectangle made me look like I had finished something. I watched the other children, who were loud and messy and happy.

From three tables away, I heard a girl’s voice. It was loud, cheerful, and completely unafraid.

"It exploded a little," she said.

I turned my head toward the source, fixing on the girl in the yellow raincoat. She was short and sturdy, with thick black curly hair piled in a messy bun that held pencils like a pencil case. Safety goggles sat on her head, and a crowd of classmates surrounded her, all laughing.

She was not perfect. She was not flawless. She was a mess, and she was happy.

My head tilted twelve degrees to the left. I did not have a name for the reading I was trying to process. I looked at her, then at my empty tray, then at the class, and finally back at my index. It was still eleven.

I wanted to know what she had learned.
pages.image: A short, sturdy girl in a big yellow raincoat and a messy bun with pencils in it laughs with friends at a lunch table, while a tall silver-white robot sits alone at a distance, watching her.
